title: Scholarship today
hookLine: al-Azhar, Najaf, Qom, Deoband, Medina, and online

lines: A LIST OF NAMES, CLIMBING BACK.
cards: A sheet of paper, handwritten, with a list of names running down it. At the bottom, a student's name. Above it, the teacher who heard the student recite and gave permission to teach.
Above that, the teacher's teacher, and another, and another, climbing back through the generations.
It's called an ijaza, a permission, and in the tradition it's how knowledge is handed on: not just from a book, but from a person who learned it from a person.

teach.b: The Qur'an gives the student's prayer in a few words. Pickthall translates it: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge."

And in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase, that whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise. So where are those paths today?
Start in Cairo, at al-Azhar, a mosque and a university where Sunni students study Qur'an, hadith, law and Arabic.
Go east to Iraq and Iran, to Najaf and Qom, cities of the hawza, the Shia seminaries, where students sit with teachers and train as scholars of law.
Then Deoband, a town in northern India with a seminary whose name is carried by schools in other countries too. Then Medina, the Prophet's own city, home to the Islamic University.
Each place has its own emphases, its own teachers and its own way of teaching, and Muslims hold different views about them. And then a new place: online.
Recorded lessons, live classes, a teacher in one country and a student in another, sometimes still ending with an ijaza given across a screen.

teach.h: A PATH TO PARADISE MADE EASY.
teach.b: Some teachers warn that a video can't correct your mistakes the way a person in the room can. Others say it opens a door that was closed to people far from any city of learning.
The old shape still holds: a student, a teacher, a text, and a question asked out loud.

how: Muslims who want to study their tradition in depth may enroll at a university or seminary such as al-Azhar, a hawza in Najaf or Qom, a madrasa in the Deobandi tradition, or the Islamic University of Medina, or join classes with a teacher online or at a local mosque.

games.q: you want to learn to recite the Qur'an well, and the nearest teacher is far away. a recorded course is free online. what do teachers say?
o: a screen is just as good, full stop.
they disagree: some warn a video can't correct you, others say it opens a door.
games.why: they disagree. some warn that only a person in the room can catch your mistakes; others say online classes reach people far from any city of learning.

practice: Think of one thing you know well, a recipe, a skill, a prayer, a way of fixing something, and ask who taught it to you, and who taught them. Go up the list as far as you can, name by name, face by face, and notice where it fades.
If you pray, say the Qur'an's short prayer for knowledge; if you don't, just hold the wish to learn.

wordCard.voice: Scholarship today. The places Muslims study their tradition now, al-Azhar, Najaf, Qom, Deoband, Medina and online, and the teacher-to-student chain they share. Today's word.
